I’ve put the complaint, the exhibits and the older company records together because I want people to be able to follow this case without having to piece it together from screenshots and replies.

That includes both sides. Korra says he received court documents, denies the allegations and says none of this happened. His denial needs to be included.

X filed its lawsuit against Immortal Snail LLC on September 28, 2026, in the Northern District of Texas. The case number is 4:26-cv-01254. Immortal Snail is the only named defendant in the federal case. Being mentioned in the complaint doesn’t automatically make someone else a defendant.

This is a civil lawsuit about contracts, suspended accounts and arbitration. X wants to stop the arbitration brought by Snail and is suing for breach of contract. There’s no judgment in the material I’ve reviewed establishing the bribery, unauthorized-access or impersonation allegations as proven. The complaint doesn’t bring a standalone RICO claim either, although RICO comes up in an earlier letter.

The complaint itself is 31 pages. The ECF 1 package I reviewed runs to 288 pages, including the cover sheet, index and 25 exhibits. Those exhibits matter because they also include Snail’s account, letters from its lawyers, contracts and commercial records. This package isn’t the entire, up-to-date court file.

One document deserves particular attention: the January 12, 2026 letter from their own lawyers.

Kevin C. Kaplan and Christopher E. Cheek, of Coffey Burlington, say they represent Immortal Snail, Moonrail Limited B.V. and Ossi Ketola. They describe Ketola as the “principal and owner” of both companies. The letter is part of Snail’s arbitration claim, included in Exhibit 25, pages 17–18.

If you have a claim or ongoing proceedings against Ketola involving Duel or CSGOEmpire, that’s a document worth putting in front of your lawyer. It gives them a specific statement from his stated representatives to consider when looking at ownership, corporate relationships and who belongs in your case. The separate companies, directors and representatives have to be considered alongside that statement.

The letter doesn’t settle personal liability, give ownership percentages or establish that one company is a subsidiary of the other. It also doesn’t prove that the companies are fictitious or their directors are acting as fronts. What it does record is how those lawyers described their clients and Ketola’s ownership.

The platforms’ own terms identify the companies:

Duel: Immortal Snail LLC, Nevis, registration L22982.
CSGOEmpire: Moonrail Limited B.V., Curaçao, registration 148182.
Payments for Moonrail may be handled by JHOLT LTD, Cyprus, registration HE393291, under an agreement between the two companies.

Moonrail also appears in DUEL’s trademark records. The official Israeli register lists it as the owner of trademark 374583, registered on May 5, 2025. In Canada, Moonrail filed DUEL application 2342187 on August 6, 2024. The Canadian record names David S. Lipkus of Lipkus Law LLP as the trademark agent and records the application as abandoned under section 36 on July 17, 2026.

That abandonment concerns the Canadian application. It doesn’t mean every DUEL trademark was cancelled or the platform stopped operating. And these records describe different jobs: owning a trademark, operating a platform, processing payments and representing a trademark applicant aren’t interchangeable roles.

The account history in X’s complaint starts in 2024, before the purchases people are discussing.

X alleges that on March 25, 2024, Ketola and Snail took control of an account using @duel, changed its email to a Moonrail mailbox and used it to promote a casino. X says it suspended the account on March 27, after which attempts to recover it involved intermediaries and access to employees. [Paragraphs 36–39.]

X also alleges that Ketola and CSGOEmpire were involved in an intrusion into @CSGORoll reported in April 2024. It cites a livestream in which, according to the complaint, Ketola celebrated what happened, mentioned “Sticky Hand” and said he worked for him. I haven’t authenticated the original video. X says it suspended @JNSAST the following day after reports of targeted harassment, disclosure of personal information and threats. [Paragraphs 28–29.]

The complaint goes on to describe what X calls bribery and unauthorized account reinstatements. It alleges that internal information about @duel was obtained in June 2024 and usernames were changed to move @monarch to another account. It also says an employee photographed internal information in July after a $1,500 offer and was fired. Further reinstatements through contractors and further suspensions followed, according to X. [Paragraphs 39, 40 and 44–49.]

There’s a company letter in this part of the file too. Exhibit 3 contains Moonrail’s July 9, 2024 authorization for Dušan Pećić to represent it. The names beneath the signatures are Lorenza Godett and Christopher van Rosberg, acting for Xecutive Corporate Management B.V., which is identified as a director of Moonrail. HLTV also named Pećić as CSGOEmpire’s marketing manager in March 2024.

The letter authorizes representation. It doesn’t authorize hacking, bribery or threats, or show that its signatories knew about the conduct X alleges.

The dates also need to stay as written. X dates Pećić’s appeal to June 28, 2024, but the authorization letter is dated July 9. Paragraph 47 then dates the rejection to July 13, 2025. I’m not going to quietly change those dates to make them line up.

Haci Isik appears as an intermediary. X says he was engaged in December 2024 to recover @duel and looked for insiders willing to reactivate or suspend accounts for money. It says he later tried to buy the handle directly, presenting an esports and FPS gaming project in February 2025. That’s X’s description of the discussions and their purpose. [Paragraphs 41–43.]

Paragraph 43 names two different payers: according to X, Moonrail paid for @duel_temp’s Premium subscription, while Immortal Snail paid for @duel itself. The person negotiating, the subscription payer and the handle buyer have different roles in that account. We don’t have the full negotiation or complete banking records in this package.

The acquisition documents total $480,000:

A $300,000 invoice for @Duel, dated March 24, 2025.
An $80,000 invoice for @Monarch, dated April 16.
A $100,000 receipt for @Castle, paid on June 3.

Snail says it paid all three. But two documents are invoices and one is a receipt, so I’m not calling them three bank payment confirmations. The @Castle receipt says “Crypto.” It gives no wallet, network, asset or transaction hash to trace. [Exhibit 25, pp. 13–15.]

A handle can move between accounts. The 2024 events and the 2025 purchases don’t establish that one person continuously owned one underlying account.

Then there’s the Grizzly section shown in the screenshot.

X describes Grizzly as a former CSGOEmpire Product Manager who fell out with Ketola. It alleges that Ketola and Snail accessed one of his accounts without authorization in February 2025, after he published internal conversations. [Paragraph 30.]

According to X, the Discord and Telegram conversations discussed accessing Israeli government email accounts and using them to ask platforms to remove competitors’ accounts, including CSGORoll. The complaint also describes discussions about wording those requests to make them look like legitimate official requests.

The original emails and their headers aren’t in the package I reviewed, and I haven’t independently verified who controlled those mailboxes. None of this establishes involvement by the Israeli government.

Paragraph 31 quotes Grizzly claiming to have more than 6.5 GB of chat exports and other evidence. In that quoted post, he said the material included plans to disclose relatives’ personal information and references to physical attacks against Stake. He also said he feared for his life and was looking for a journalist to receive the files.

The full archive isn’t here. His statement that he had it doesn’t tell us whether he delivered it to X, a journalist or an authority.

Paragraph 32 describes a video conversation between “Gr1zzly” and “Monarch,” whom X identifies as Ketola. X attributes to Monarch references to Bosnian mafia contacts, plans for kidnappings and possible murders, obtaining personal information, services involving violence and statements about mutilations.

Those are exceptionally serious allegations. I haven’t authenticated the original video, and I don’t have independent evidence establishing that the acts described were carried out. I’m reporting what X attributes to that conversation.

Paragraph 33 describes another conversation, on Telegram, about using government emails to get accounts removed, with language involving escalation and violence. Here the complaint calls the participant “Ossi” and says he is presumably Ossi Ketola. “Presumably” is in the document. It stays in this account too.

X says one of Grizzly’s accounts was taken over, had its biography changed from “Ex-CSGOEmpire” to a message saying it had been seized by @theJNSAST, then was used to promote Duel. It also cites @monarchlawyer announcing an account takeover. A username containing “lawyer” doesn’t establish that the person using it is one. [Paragraph 34.]

Korra expressly denies these events in the post being quoted. That denial belongs alongside the allegations. I also couldn’t retrieve the original links in footnotes 15–18 in readable form, so the complaint and screenshots aren’t a substitute for authenticating the underlying material.

X makes a technical claim as well. Footnote 15 says @fastschitzobear, @CSGOEmpire, @CSGOEmpireV2, @duel and @monarch used the same Known Device Token. X treats that as evidence of previous access through the same device or browser and an indication of collaboration. Paragraph 50 also refers to matches involving devices, software, identifiers, cookies and financial accounts.

The complete logs and dates needed to check that conclusion aren’t in the package. A shared device doesn’t tell us who wrote a particular message, or whether the overlap happened before or after an account takeover.

There are further allegations about accounts critical of the business.

Paragraph 35 describes a trademark complaint with allegedly manipulated documents against a former CSGOEmpire social media manager. That role shouldn’t automatically be treated as the Product Manager role attributed to Grizzly. In paragraph 52, X alleges that Isik offered in June 2025 to find insiders who would suspend accounts critical of Ketola and his companies. These remain allegations in the material reviewed.

X says it suspended @duel, @monarch and @castle, along with related accounts, around October 21, 2025. It alleges that requests impersonating a US law firm followed, as did a $300,000 offer to an employee to reactivate accounts. Exhibits 1 and 2 contain the November letters X disputes. Paragraph 56 doesn’t give the exact date of the alleged offer.

There are two different $300,000 figures here. The first is the invoiced purchase price for @Duel. The second is an alleged bribe in a later incident. They shouldn’t be merged.

Paragraph 58 describes a May 2026 request that X says impersonated the Malaysian police, followed by complaints in India. The exhibits show the request fields, but they don’t authenticate the senders. I’m leaving out the names of people who may themselves have been impersonated.

X mentions Arya A. when linking an email identifier used in requests with one in billing documents. That is X’s attribution. It doesn’t establish a company position or authorship of every communication.

Snail’s side is in the file too, and it deserves to be read.

Its arbitration claim says it paid for the handles and then lost access without an adequate explanation, harming its business, reputation and commercial expectations. It wants the accounts restored and compensation. It also raises possible interference by competitors or an X shareholder connected to competitors. The material I reviewed neither names that shareholder nor establishes that theory. [Exhibit 25, pp. 4–8.]

Snail started arbitration in April 2026. X says the relevant contracts require disputes to go to Texas courts. Mohamed F. Sweify was appointed arbitrator in July. Kaplan and Cheek attended an August preliminary hearing; X had said it wouldn’t participate and maintained that position. The arbitration order put jurisdiction first.

Part of the dispute is which terms apply. The 2024 handle-transfer terms select a Texas forum, reserve suspension rights and include a $100 limit on liability. Snail relies on the October 2025 Marketplace terms, which include arbitration subject to US residency. How those terms apply here is a question in the case, not something this post resolves.

X’s September letter mentioned possible legal actions, including RICO. That doesn’t turn this into a filed RICO claim, a criminal prosecution or an established FBI investigation.

The federal complaint names Caitlin A. Halpern and Lauryn E. Bennett of Gibbs & Bruns, and Charles W. Fillmore of Brown Pruitt, as X’s lawyers. The public docket records the case’s reassignment to Reed O’Connor on September 30. A lawyer’s representation of a party doesn’t make them responsible for the conduct being disputed.

The older company records help explain the business relationships. They need to be read with their own limits: these are supplied historical copies, and I haven’t independently certified every file’s authenticity or confirmed its official receipt. The X lawsuit doesn’t authenticate the rest of the archive.

An August 2023 organizational chart shows Ossi owning 100% of Moonrail and Moonrail owning 100% of JHOLT. That tells us what the chart records at that time; it isn’t a current ownership certificate. [D026.]

Moonrail’s shareholders’ register goes further back. The copy marked D027 reproduces a certification dated July 29, 2024. It records Xecutive Corporate Management B.V. subscribing for all 10,000 shares on October 1, 2018, then transferring them the next day. That initial shareholding is a separate role from its later corporate administration work.

The register lists these corporate holdings from October 2, 2018, and their later transfers:

JPellikka Oy, Finland, 2881789-9: 13.65%, later recorded under Day Star Enterprises OÜ, Estonia, 14630609.
Hiirijoki & Partners Oy, Finland, 2887371-9: 12.50%, later recorded under Rotten Apples OÜ, Estonia, 14631261.
create.repeat Oy, Finland, 2662670-6: 13.65%, later recorded under Simple Holdings OÜ, Estonia, 14635334.

It dates those three transfers to December 17, 2018. It then records Ketola, who already held 44.80%, acquiring the remaining 55.20% on November 13, 2019. That remaining stake consists of the three company holdings totaling 39.80%, plus an individual holding of 15.40%.

Those entries don’t tell us the purchase price or show the payments. They also don’t make those companies current owners of Duel. [D027, pp. 3–4.]

The Estonian public register confirms the companies’ identities and gives these dates:

Day Star: registered December 21, 2018; deleted from the register August 13, 2021.
Rotten Apples: registered December 27, 2018; deleted September 8, 2021.
Simple Holdings: registered January 4, 2019; deleted November 26, 2021.

All three registration dates are later than the December 17 transfer date in Moonrail’s book. That needs an explanation from the underlying documents. I can’t resolve the legally effective transfer dates from these records or call the discrepancy proof of forgery. The public company records establish those companies’ existence; the link to Moonrail’s shares comes from the supplied shareholders’ register.

Finland’s register also shows that JPellikka Oy became Veivi Ventures Oy on January 18, 2023. A later name change doesn’t establish a present-day stake in Moonrail.

There’s more on the earlier funding in a November 14, 2025 letter addressed to the Curaçao Gaming Authority. Moonrail says its initial funding came from Ketola’s earlier business activities through Global Vault oy and the distribution of that company’s assets after liquidation.

Global Vault’s Finnish registration number is 2793380-4. It was registered on November 9, 2016, and dissolved on April 1, 2019. The register confirms those facts. The explanation connecting its funds to Moonrail comes from Moonrail’s letter; it isn’t bank verification and doesn’t establish that Global Vault operated CSGOEmpire. [D050, pp. 1–3.]

The historical PRH/Virre extract issued on August 14, 2026 lists Ossi Eemeli Ketola as Global Vault’s board member and managing director from November 9, 2016 to July 5, 2018. It lists Satu Maarit Ketola as a deputy board member over the same period, and Lari Hiirijoki as a procurist, meaning a holder of a commercial power of attorney, from November 2017. His later appointment as liquidator was registered on July 5, 2018.

Those are documented business roles. They don’t establish family relationships or positions for those other individuals at today’s operators. [Global Vault PRH/Virre extract, pp. 1–3.]

The January 18, 2019 liquidator’s report in D050 identifies Ketola as holding all 100 shares and the rights to Global Vault’s asset distribution. Lari Hiirijoki signs as liquidator. This adds to the ownership and funding history, but it still doesn’t supply the records of transfers between the people and companies involved. [D050, pp. 10–11.]

There’s a one-year difference between two documents that I’m keeping visible. Moonrail’s November 2025 letter says Ketola owned 100% of Moonrail from November 13, 2018. The shareholders’ register puts his purchase of the final 55.20% on November 13, 2019. I don’t have enough to settle which date is correct.

The same letter gives Moonrail’s licensing account: Cyberluck N.V. in 2018, Antillephone N.V. in 2021, then the Gaming Control Board/Curaçao Gaming Authority framework. That is Moonrail’s account of its sublicensing and licensing history. It doesn’t establish permission to operate everywhere, and it can’t simply be applied to Immortal Snail. [D050, p. 1.]

The February 2025 assessment in the archive identifies missing documentation and recommends conditions covering management identification, anti-money-laundering measures, responsible gambling, territorial access and media policy. These are recommendations, not a sanction or proof that every proposed condition was imposed. [D029.]

A later business plan, identified in the archive as October 30, 2025, names Irene Rosenblatt as CEO, Matt Tanner as CFO and Sampsa Saarela as CTO. It names Rokas Daugirdas as compliance manager and Pearl Reiph as MLRO, the money-laundering reporting role. Xecutive is described as the board, with the CEO responsible for daily operations and reporting to it. Those are the roles this historical plan gives them. I haven’t verified that they still hold them, and the titles don’t prove involvement in X’s allegations. [D041, pp. 1–2 and 4–5.]

Moonrail’s advertising policy is worth reading in full as well. Version 1.0, dated May 29, 2025, requires prior advertising review, influencer agreements, sponsorship disclosure and territorial controls. It prohibits presenting gambling as a solution to financial difficulties, associating it with violence or dangerous behavior, and using content or influencers that appeal to minors. Advertising materials require compliance approval. Moonrail and its agents are also prohibited from offering players credit or loans to gamble. [D037, pp. 4–6.]

Those are written rules for Moonrail at that date. To assess a particular campaign against them, we’d still need to check the campaign itself, when it ran and which policy applied. Having a policy doesn’t tell us how it was followed in every case.

The archive also contains an August 1, 2025 response attributed to Xecutive on Moonrail’s behalf about Coffeezilla. It denies bribery. It says former managers proposed investigating a competitor without senior authorization, denies asking anyone to suppress or change coverage of Moonrail, and says the people who acted without authorization were removed. They aren’t named. The letter describes the owner as providing strategic guidance, separate from operational campaigns. That response needs to accompany the allegation. [D038.]

The August and November 2025 letters both present Xecutive Corporate Management B.V. as a director of Moonrail. Their signature blocks name Analissa Heiland and Lorenza Godett as its representatives. That establishes how they are presented in those letters, not participation in the alleged conduct. These letters and the other historical copies remain subject to the authenticity and date limitations explained above. [D038, p. 2; D050, p. 2.]

The regulatory decisions have their own official sources.

Spain’s decision ES/2025/011 imposes a €5 million fine and a four-year disqualification from conducting gambling activities on Moonrail for operating without the required Spanish authorization. It identifies CSGOEmpire and orders the activity to stop. The DGOJ announced the sanction in November 2025. I haven’t verified whether it was paid or the outcome of any appeals.

Sweden prohibited Moonrail from providing gambling without the required license in a decision dated November 2, 2023. Denmark’s official list includes https://t.co/wm4kIZPtIu among the domains blocked by court order in July 2023.

Those decisions apply to the countries and dates they cover. They don’t prove X’s allegations of bribery or unauthorized access. A declared Curaçao or Anjouan license doesn’t establish permission to operate in every other market either.

For people with disputes over balances or affiliate earnings, the terms themselves also matter. CSGOEmpire’s terms, marked as updated on July 7, 2026, promise withdrawals even when an account is closed and, where necessary, compensation for unclaimed referral earnings or rewards. They also contain exceptions and restrictions for abuse, self-referrals, dormant accounts and reversed trades. Any particular withholding needs to be checked against the terms that applied, the clause relied on and the account records. The page alone doesn’t prove a breach in someone’s case.

I also need to be open about my own position. I’ve filed a police complaint over a separate dispute. It records my allegations; it isn’t a judgment proving them. X’s case doesn’t settle my claims either. I’m leaving out amounts that still need reconciliation and keeping the two proceedings separate.

What we have here is a civil complaint, Snail’s arbitration claim, commercial records, a letter from lawyers describing Ketola’s ownership of both operators, historical company documents and official regulatory decisions. The most serious allegations in the complaint haven’t been established as proven in the material I’ve reviewed.

If I’ve got a document, page or date wrong, point me to it. I’ll correct it. I’ll also include responses supported by documents.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

DHS just yeeted DeepSeek out of the entire federal civilian tech stack, effective immediately.
The absolute irony of DHS banning DSH is pure poetry 😂
The order covers DeepSeek itself, its affiliates, and any third-party wrappers running their tech. The feds are spooked about prompts pinging back to Chinese servers, telemetry snooping, and local vulnerabilities. Agencies have 60 days to beg CISA for a waiver if their workflow is cooked without it.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

🚨Delhi HC Just Drew the Line on AI Deepfakes and It Changes Everything

Delhi HC’s order in Anil Kumar Tiwari (Aniruddhacharya) v. John Doe (Ashok Kumar & Ors.), CS(COMM) 336/2026 is more than a takedown of memes and deepfakes, it signals a structural shift in how India is preparing for the AI-driven future.

Key aspects of the case:

• Plaintiff: Anil Kumar Tiwari, widely known as Aniruddhacharya Ji Maharaj ("Pookie Baba")

• Defendants: John Doe (Ashok Kumar & Ors.), covering anonymous creators along with intermediaries like Meta, Google, and X

• The Problem: Circulation of AI-generated deepfakes, doctored videos, fake endorsements, and distorted spiritual discourse violating personality rights

• Court Order: Complete restraint on creating or sharing any content replicating the plaintiff’s name, voice, image, or mannerisms without authorization

• Intermediary Directions: Meta, X, and Google directed to remove, disable access, and take down all flagged content immediately

The Court (Justice Tushar Rao Gedela, 30 March 2026) granted an ex-parte ad-interim injunction, recognizing that a person’s identity is not public property but a legally enforceable asset.

The mood of this judgment is unmistakably urgent, protective, and corrective. What was once brushed off as meme culture is now being treated as structured digital harm amplified by AI.

Key judicial observations:

• Personality Rights Recognized:

The Court affirmed that a public figure’s identity carries enforceable personality and publicity rights

• Irreparable Loss:

Unauthorized AI usage causes serious reputational damage that cannot be monetarily compensated

• "Love for Delhi" Remark:

Justice Gedela interestingly questioned why such cases consistently prefer Delhi HC jurisdiction, even when defendants are anonymous, hinting at forum concentration in tech-IP disputes

What makes this ruling significant:

• Personality = IP asset
Identity is now treated as an economic and legal right, expanding India’s IP framework

• Dynamic enforcement model 
Not a one-time order, but continuous takedown authority against evolving content

• John Doe mechanism
Adapts law to the anonymous, decentralized nature of AI misuse

• Deepfakes legally elevated
No longer trivial, now recognized as causing irreversible real-world harm

The AI Reality Check:
AI itself is neutral, but its misuse is not.

Positive side:

• Creativity at scale
• Education and accessibility
• Digital economy expansion
Negative side (highlighted here):
• Fake endorsements and scams
• Reputation manipulation
• Synthetic misinformation
• Identity theft through voice and face cloning

This case shows how AI has blurred the line between satire and synthetic deception.

Impact on India’s IP & Legal Ecosystem:

This ruling strengthens:

• Recognition of persona as intellectual property
• Platform accountability (Meta, Google, X as enforcement layers)
• Early foundations of AI governance frameworks
• Evolution toward structured digital identity protection laws

It also aligns with broader regulatory momentum around AI and intermediary responsibility.
What this means for the future:

We are entering a phase where:

• Every public personality becomes a protectable digital asset

• AI systems will require consent and compliance layers

• Courts will increasingly define boundaries of AI usage

• Deepfake regulation will become unavoidable

In simple terms:

Your face, voice, and personality are becoming your most valuable IP.

Conclusion:

This is not just about one individual.
It is about protecting human identity in an era of synthetic reality.

The message is clear:

Innovation is welcome, exploitation is not.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

### Summary
The PR does two related things:

1. **Documents and drifts-checks branch rulesets** — Adds checked-in JSON snapshots (`.github/rulesets/main.json` and `releases.json`) plus a README. These capture the active rules for `main` (merge queue + protections) and release branches: 1 human approving review, code-owner review, dismiss stale, require last-push approval, thread resolution, extra approval for unattributed changes, no force-push/deletion, and a short list of required status checks. A new `scripts/check-ruleset-snapshots.mjs` (called from the existing required-checks-drift workflow) compares them to the live GitHub API and opens/updates a drift issue.

2. **Enforces review-ready PR descriptions** — Adds a required CI job `🧐 PR summary review` (`pr-summary-review` in `ci.yml`) that runs on `pull_request` and `merge_group`. The script `scripts/check-pr-review-readiness.mjs` parses the PR body for non-placeholder content under `## What changed?` and a completed verification item (checked box or filled “Other check”) under `## How did you check it?`. It writes a job summary, emits `::error::` annotations, and fails closed. Bot/AI checks are explicitly documented as *not* counting toward the human approval required by OpenSSF Scorecard Code-Review.

Supporting changes include inventory/required-check updates, runner label moves to `ubuntu-26.04` (with an `actionlint.yaml` allow-list), and small e2e trigger/required-status adjustments so the summary job and rulesets stay consistent.

### Strengths
- Clear separation of concerns: automated completeness gate vs. human approval. The README and job summary both state that bots do not replace human review — good for Scorecard.
- Fail-closed on merge-queue events (fetches the PR body via `gh api` using the queue ref; throws if it can’t).
- Solid unit tests covering placeholders, HTML comments, Windows line endings, duplicate headings, asterisk vs. dash list markers, the “I said which checks I did not run” exemption, and merge-queue ref parsing.
- Snapshot + drift workflow is a maintainable way to keep rulesets documented without relying solely on the GitHub UI.
- The readiness parser is pragmatic (strips comments, ignores common template placeholders, requires real content).

### Issues / questions
1. **Required-check surface area changed significantly.**  
   `.github/required-checks.json` is deleted and several e2e gates (`e2e-scale`, `e2e-examples`, `e2e-platforms`, `e2e-journeys`, etc.) flip from `"required": true` to `false` in the inventory. The new ruleset snapshots only list `example-e2e`, `windows-smoke`, and `🧐 PR summary review`.  
   Is the reduction intentional (e.g., moving to rulesets and slimmed required set for Scorecard/merge-queue reasons)? If so, the commit messages / PR body should call it out more clearly so reviewers don’t miss the policy change.

2. **`ubuntu-26.04` runner label.**  
   The change is widespread. Confirm the label is available on GitHub-hosted runners (or your self-hosted pool) and that actionlint’s allow-list is sufficient. If 26.04 is still preview/future, this could break CI until the image is stable.

3. **Ruleset snapshots vs. inventory.**  
   The snapshots hard-code a small required-check list. The inventory still tracks more jobs (now mostly non-required). Make sure the drift check and any “required” expectations stay aligned, and that adding a new required check still follows the documented “merge the workflow first, then update the live ruleset” order.

4. **Parser edge cases (minor).**  
   - A one-line non-placeholder summary is enough; a malicious or low-effort author can still satisfy it. Acceptable for a completeness gate, but worth noting.  
   - Section extraction takes the *first* matching heading (tested). Fine, but a later real section would be ignored if an earlier placeholder one exists.  
   - “Other check:” matching is case-sensitive in one path and case-insensitive in another; the tests cover the common forms, but a quick consistency pass wouldn’t hurt.

5. **Scope.**  
   Runner upgrades, e2e required-status flips, and the readiness gate are bundled. If the runner change is independent, splitting it would make review and rollback easier. Not a blocker if everything is green and intentional.

### Verdict
**Approve with minor comments.** The core idea (documented rulesets + a lightweight PR-completeness gate that explicitly preserves human review) is sound, well-tested, and aligned with Scorecard Code-Review. The main things to confirm before merge are:

- That the reduction in required status checks is deliberate and documented.
- That `ubuntu-26.04` is usable in your environment.

Once those are acknowledged (or adjusted), this looks ready.

This video is said to be from 2009. Look at how the Election Commission of India functioned then, and compare it with what is happening today.

The Election Commission freely encouraged citizens to exercise their voting rights. Its advertisements highlighted the problems people faced in everyday life, including corruption, poor education, inadequate healthcare, crumbling infrastructure and bad governance, and reminded them that the power to change these conditions lay in their votes.

The central purpose was to promote universal adult franchise, encourage electoral participation and increase voter turnout.

Watch this advertisement carefully. It clearly conveys the message that if the government has failed to deliver good governance, the citizens have the power to change it through elections.

Did anyone accuse the Election Commission of being biased or campaigning against the government? Did the government have to rush to its defence? Or was the Election Commission simply exercising its constitutional independence?

In 2013, following the Supreme Court’s intervention, VVPAT was introduced to strengthen transparency and build confidence among voters and political parties. The Supreme Court recognised that an independently verifiable paper trail was indispensable to free and fair elections.

Now look at what is happening.

When questions were raised about the extraordinary increase in reported voter turnout after 5 PM, political parties and citizens sought access to CCTV footage and election records.

The Punjab and Haryana High Court directed the Election Commission to provide the relevant footage and records. What followed?

Instead of making election records more accessible, the Central Government amended Rule 93 of the Conduct of Election Rules in December 2024, on the Election Commission’s recommendation, restricting public access to CCTV footage and other electronic election records.

Subsequently, the Election Commission introduced instructions permitting the destruction of CCTV footage and other recordings after just 45 days where no election petition had been filed.

Why should evidence relating to the conduct of elections be made inaccessible and then destroyed when transparency is precisely what establishes public confidence?

The Supreme Court rejected the demand for 100% VVPAT verification in 2024. But what is the purpose of an independently verifiable paper trail if its comprehensive verification is resisted? The very purpose of introducing VVPAT was to strengthen public confidence in election results.

Why Were 4.8 Million Names Deleted From The Delhi SIR? We've Found Out!

Propaganda appears to be spreading around two main issues regarding the Delhi SIR process. The first is the issuance of notices, and the second is the deletion of approximately 4.8 million names from the voter list. Watch this video to find out the real truth behind both these controversies!

The removal of nearly 4.8 million names (roughly a third of the total electorate) from Delhi's draft electoral rolls during the first phase of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) has sparked intense political controversy. According to data and statements from the Election Commission of India (ECI) and various investigative platforms, the massive exclusion occurred due to several administrative, technological, and systematic factors.

According to Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, the nationwide SIR drive was implemented to clean up India’s massive voter database by removing voters who are no longer eligible, ensuring that taxpayer-funded welfare benefits reach only legitimate, verified citizens. 

Nationwide, more than 130 million names have been removed. In Delhi, the official grounds for flagging these 4.8 million names include:

• Absent and Shifted Voters: Deletions of electors who have relocated or could not be traced at their registered addresses during administrative field checks.

• Logical Discrepancies and Database Glitches: Millions of names were flagged for technical irregularities, missing data fields, or a lack of proper digital "mapping" with legacy voter data.

• Unsubmitted or Undigitised Forms: During Phase I, voters were required to fill out forms linking themselves back to historical base records. Approximately 4.76 million forms were left un-digitised or unlinked by the initial administrative deadlines.
Credit : The Pamphlet.

Machine-Readable Electoral Rolls
Before: ECI declined to provide readable rolls, citing privacy concerns.

Form 6 Declaration
Before: Required parental mapping and lineage proof for new voter registrations.

Voter Verification
Before: Deleted voters had to travel to the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO) office to re-enrol.

Bulk Deletions Under Form 7

SIR vs SSR
Before: Special Intensive Revision (SIR) involved house-to-house enumeration with citizenship documents, leading to ∼5.18 crore deletions.
Now: Special Summary Revision (SSR) is being applied for left-out voters in 17 states where SIR was completed.

Transparency & Disclosure
Before: Electoral roll supplements were shared as non-readable image PDFs with limited incremental sharing.
Now: Readable PDFs with addition/deletion supplements are shared, plus a weekly claims list on the CEO website.

text:
India has a strange problem.

The technology to connect its most remote villages already exists. The companies are ready. The infrastructure is being built.

But the government still won't let them switch it on.

SpaceX's @Starlink received its telecom license in June 2025, followed by space regulatory approval a month later.

It has established 20 ground stations in India, agreed to local data storage, and accepted extensive security and monitoring requirements.

Yet it still cannot sell a single subscription.

Meanwhile, more than 1,800 villages in northeastern India had no mobile signal at all as of February.

Think about that.

We're talking about communities where building traditional cell towers or laying fiber could take years. Satellite internet could dramatically change their access to education, healthcare, and economic opportunities.

And Starlink isn't the only company stuck. Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio's satellite ventures are also waiting.

That's the bigger problem.

When every major operator gets trapped in the same approval process, perhaps it's time to question the process itself.

National security matters. India has every right to protect its infrastructure and citizens.

But security reviews need clear standards, accountability, and deadlines.

India wants to become a global technology powerhouse.

Then why are people in its remote villages still waiting for permission to join the digital world?

Connectivity should not be held hostage by bureaucracy.

quotedTweet.text:
Starlink has an Indian license, 20 ground stations on Indian soil, and a promise to keep Indian user data in India. What it doesn't have is permission to switch on.

Thousands of Indian villages still have no 4G. In the Northeast alone, more than 1,800 had no mobile signal of any kind as of February, most of them in Arunachal Pradesh. These are the places satellite internet is built for: mountain villages, islands, flood zones, anywhere a tower or a fiber line takes years and a lot of money to arrive.

Starlink has done what India asked. It got its telecom license in June 2025 and space regulator approval a month later. It built India-specific security controls, agreed to keep data local, and has been reporting the names, addresses and coordinates of its test terminals to the government every two weeks. It operates in more than 150 countries. In India it still can't sell a single subscription, and the company is now talking about early 2027.

New Delhi says nobody is being singled out, since Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio's satellite venture are stuck at the same stage. I believe that, and I don't think it helps. When three licensed operators, two of them backed by India's biggest telecom groups, can't clear security review after more than a year of trials, that tells you the process has no deadline. It doesn't tell you it's thorough.

The security concerns are real. Indian agencies have been rattled by smuggled terminals turning up in border areas, and India is entitled to lawful interception, local data storage and an emergency shutoff. Starlink has already signed up for all of it. The answer to a misused terminal is enforcement, not keeping the service dark for everyone who would use it legally.

Elon Musk has been blunt, calling the delay "a crime against the people of India" and asking, "Is Ambani the real boss of India?" You don't need to buy the whole oligarch theory to see his point. Reliance spent months lobbying for spectrum auctions that would have favored deep-pocketed incumbents. The government sided with Starlink on that one, which is to its credit. Now it needs to finish the job.

India can keep every security power it wants and still let a kid in Arunachal get online. Right now it's choosing not to.

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

1/ From FY22-23 to FY24-25, India collected ₹1,096 crore in crypto TDS.

Meanwhile, uncollected TDS since the regime began in July 2022 is estimated at ~₹19,049 crore.

The reason: ~95% of Indian crypto trading now happens on offshore platforms that deduct no TDS, around ₹9 lakh crore in FY25-26 alone. Factoring in capital gains tax, the estimated loss to the exchequer is ~₹57,147 crore, and it's growing every year.

A recent TIOL Knowledge Foundation report says fixing the tax design, rather than more enforcement against a shrinking base, could bring in up to ₹1.81 lakh crore in capital gains tax over 5 years. 

Sharing some interesting insights from the report below.  🧵

4/ Root cause #1: the 1% TDS makes following the rules the expensive option

>Every transaction on an Indian exchange attracts a 1% TDS. Active traders feel that cost on every trade, while offshore platforms deduct nothing.
>So volume moves offshore, mostly through P2P (peer-to-peer) trading.

5/ Root cause #2: a legal gap offshore platforms rely on
In P2P trading. An offshore platform matches buyers and sellers, but the rupees move directly between Indian bank accounts. Because the platform isn't registered in India and never handles the money, it argues it has no duty to deduct TDS.

That's why blocking websites alone didn't work. When FIU-IND blocked 25 offshore exchanges in Oct'25, users didn't come back to Indian exchanges. They moved to P2P on platforms that were still accessible.

Narendra Modi employs the oldest and most tried-and-true political trick in the book to maintain control of media outlets and shape the dominant narrative. The government has used 195,000 social media takedown orders to systematically suppress online content and voices. Journalists have been detained and prevented from freely reporting, and the Prime Minister has strategically avoided holding solo press conferences where he could be questioned directly. Throughout this process, accountability mechanisms have been deliberately dismantled and destroyed, effectively silencing opposition voices and preventing meaningful dissent from reaching the public sphere.

Statement against arbitrary content takedown and account restrictions faced by public representatives and journalists

Earlier today, @Meta restricted the Instagram accounts (“Platform”) of @AamAadmiParty (AAP), its national convener @ArvindKejriwal, and Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear), co-founder of @AltNews. 

Over the past week, along with these instances, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also recorded several instances of content takedowns faced by media organisations including @PeekTV_in, cartoonists such as @cartoonistrrs and @cartoonistvish, and @SauravDassss - @Cockroachisback's spokesperson.

According to the publicly available information, the affected posts were restricted pursuant to the “legal requests” received by the Platform. In many cases, users are provided little or no meaningful explanation about the legal or factual basis of the restriction or what steps they can take to challenge the decision. Such opaque moderation practices undermine users’ ability to understand how platform policies are enforced and make it difficult to distinguish between legitimate moderation and arbitrary or inconsistent decision-making. This is especially concerning where the affected content relates to political expression, criticism of public authorities, or peaceful protest, all of which occupy a central place in democratic discourse.

The Supreme Court of India upheld the constitutionality of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”), on the basis that the statutory framework required that blocking orders be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. By contrast, in most of these cases, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has consistently advocated against these practices. We are concerned that this takedown drive is contrary to the rule of law and to India’s constitutional commitment to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

While private platforms are not directly bound by the Constitution in the same manner as the State, their content moderation decisions increasingly influence the digital spaces in which democratic participation takes place. This places a heightened responsibility on platforms to ensure that their moderation processes are transparent, consistently applied, and accompanied by adequate procedural safeguards, including notice, reasons for enforcement actions, and effective mechanisms for review. At the same time, any direction issued by public authorities requiring platforms to restrict lawful online speech must comply with constitutional safeguards and the legal procedures prescribed under Indian law. Informal or opaque restrictions on political speech or press freedom undermine public trust and democratic accountability.

In light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls for the following:

- Immediate disclosure of all takedown orders issued to platforms, including specific reasons and legal justifications.

- Strict adherence to the procedural safeguards laid out under Section 69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules, under the IT Act, which were upheld by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India.

- Notices received by social media intermediaries to be sent to every user affected to ensure transparency.

- Strengthening of independent oversight and appellate mechanisms to ensure that users can effectively challenge unlawful restrictions.

- Greater transparency from platforms regarding the number, nature, source, and outcome of governmental requests/orders for content removal and account restriction.

ONE GOVERNMENT BLOCKING ORDER EVERY 68 SECONDS — IS INDIA'S DIGITAL DEMOCRACY UNDER THREAT?

Pause for a moment. In the five months from March to July 2026, nearly 1.95 lakh government-backed blocking orders were sent to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, according to data reported by The Indian Express.

That is approximately 1,275 orders every day. One every 68 seconds.

This is not a trivial administrative statistic. It raises a fundamental democratic question: who decides what citizens are allowed to see, discuss and criticise online?

🚨 THE NUMBERS DEMAND PUBLIC SCRUTINY

* Instagram received nearly 1 lakh orders.

* Facebook received around 80,000.

* YouTube received nearly 15,000.

* Meta's two platforms—Instagram and Facebook—accounted for roughly nine out of every ten orders directed to these three platforms.

For comparison, RTI information previously reported by The Indian Express showed 2,312 blocking orders sent through the Sahyog portal to 19 platforms between October 2024 and October 2025.

The scale of the subsequent increase deserves a detailed public explanation.

THE MOST DISTURBING QUESTION: CAN A MACHINE REMOVE OUR VOICE WITHOUT MEANINGFUL HUMAN REVIEW?

According to The Indian Express, Meta integrated its API with the government's Sahyog portal to comply with a shortened takedown deadline. The report says this enabled government-flagged content to be removed automatically, without a separate human review by the company.

Automation may make administration faster. But speed is not the same as justice.

What happens if an order is mistaken, overbroad or insufficiently justified? Who checks whether the content actually violates the law? How quickly can an ordinary citizen challenge the decision and restore lawful speech?

A system that can silence first and explain later needs exceptionally strong safeguards.

📢 WHY THIS MATTERS TO EVERY CITIZEN

The reported orders coincided with student protests against examination-paper leaks at Delhi's Jantar Mantar. The reporting also described takedowns affecting posts concerning the government's ethanol-blending policy and the West Bengal elections.

The presence of a takedown order does not, by itself, prove unlawful censorship. Governments have legitimate duties to address unlawful content, and the law permits restrictions in defined circumstances.

But criticism of the government, peaceful protest, investigative journalism and political disagreement must not be casually treated as threats merely because they are uncomfortable for those in power.

India's constitutional commitment to freedom of speech cannot survive on assurances alone. It requires lawful orders, transparent procedures, independent scrutiny and effective remedies.

⚖️ THE LAW MUST NOT BECOME A SHORTCUT AROUND DUE PROCESS

The reporting distinguishes the takedown mechanism associated with Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act from the separate blocking framework under Section 69A.

These are not interchangeable provisions. Their legal basis, procedures and safeguards matter. The public deserves clarity about which authority issued each order, what legal grounds were invoked and what opportunity affected users had to challenge it.

OUR DEMANDS

1. Publish regular, platform-wise statistics on government takedown orders, their legal grounds and their outcomes.
2. Ensure meaningful human and legal review of disputed or ambiguous directions.
3. Give affected users clear notice, subject to narrowly justified exceptions, and an effective appeal mechanism.
4. Disclose the safeguards governing automated integration between government portals and social-media platforms.
5. Ensure that peaceful dissent, journalism and legitimate political criticism are not suppressed through vague or overbroad directions.
6. Enable independent judicial scrutiny wherever legality or fundamental rights are contested.

India cannot call itself the world's largest democracy while treating transparency about restrictions on public speech as optional.

THE ISSUE IS NOT WHETHER GOVERNMENTS CAN ENFORCE THE LAW. THE ISSUE IS WHETHER THEY CAN DO SO WITHOUT ACCOUNTABILITY.

A democracy must protect citizens from unlawful content—but it must also protect citizens' right to question the state.

When posts disappear, citizens deserve to know why. When orders are issued, the public deserves to know under what authority. And when lawful speech is wrongly removed, there must be a meaningful remedy.

Digital India must not become a system in which technology makes silencing citizens easier than answering them.

UPDATE: 14-year-old e-bike rider dies; West Melbourne store owner now charged with second-degree murder

The 14-year-old boy police say was intentionally struck by a West Melbourne store owner last week has died, and the man accused of hitting him is now charged with second-degree murder.

With the family's consent, the West Melbourne Police Department has identified the teen as Hunter Russey of West Melbourne.

According to police, the case began around 4:30 a.m. on Tuesday, October 13, when 32-year-old Kavan Vishnubhai Patel, who owns the Corner Store at 100 South Wickham Road, received an alarm alert and saw on surveillance video that the store's front glass door had been broken. Patel told officers he saw someone leave the area on an e-bike.

Police say Patel followed the rider in his vehicle and intentionally struck him along Cocoanut Grove Avenue after the encounter at the store had ended. Investigators say Patel left Hunter on the side of the road without rendering aid, returned to the store, and did not tell responding officers he had hit him. Hunter was later found unresponsive in a roadside ditch.

Hunter was taken to Holmes Regional Medical Center as a trauma alert with severe injuries and was later transferred to Orlando Health Arnold Palmer Hospital for Children, where he remained on life support.

According to police, Hunter's family made the decision to remove him from life support on the evening of Saturday, October 17. He died at 11:46 p.m. His family has chosen to donate his organs to help others.

Patel was originally charged with aggravated battery and leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. Following Hunter's death, investigators obtained an arrest warrant, and Patel was rearrested just after 10 a.m. Sunday. He is now charged with second-degree murder and is being held at the Brevard County Jail without bond.

The West Melbourne Police Department offered condolences to Hunter's family and friends and said it will continue working the case and provide prosecutors with the evidence needed to move forward.

The family has asked that the public respect their privacy.

Details:
⚠️ My laptop was remotely controlled for 5 days in short bursts of time, and the tool they used was legitimate IT software.

Last week a known contact sent me an "E-statement" file. I opened it. Nothing seemed to happen.

Over the next few days my screen would suddenly go BLACK, the mouse moved by itself, and when the screen came back after a minute my programs had been closed. Someone was operating my computer behind a black screen. Only this happened, nothing else. This pattern continued for 2 days, and I started to dig.

What we found:
🔹 The file was a zip → a .vhd disk image → "E-statement（1).exe". Look closely: that "（" is a special Unicode bracket, used to fool filters.
🔹 It was digitally signed with a real (but expired, likely stolen) company certificate, so Windows showed it as "verified".
🔹 It silently installed @manageengine  Endpoint Central, a legitimate IT-management tool used by companies, connected to the attacker's own server. Antivirus didn't flag it, because it's real software.
🔹 The attacker used its remote-control "privacy mode" to blank my screen while they worked, including in the middle of the night once.
🔹 The agent protected itself: uninstalling asked for a code I didn't have, and its driver blocked deletion. I had to remove it in Safe Mode.

👉 Lessons:
1. "Sent by someone I trust" ≠ safe. Their account may be hacked. Confirm by phone first.
2. A bank statement is a PDF, never an .exe, .vhd, .iso or .zip with a program inside.
3. "Verified publisher" does not mean safe.
4. Black screen + mouse moving on its own = someone is remotely controlling your PC. Disconnect the internet immediately.
5. Check Settings → Apps for remote tools you didn't install: ManageEngine/Zoho UEMS, AnyDesk, TeamViewer, UltraViewer, RustDesk, ScreenConnect, etc.
